title: Judging tailoring decisions
blurb: Judge whether a tailoring decision fits the project or breaks the method, and give the reason that explains it.
question: A managing director proposes acting as both executive and project manager to save time on a fast-moving launch. Is this appropriate tailoring, and why?

teach.h: Fit the method, keep the principles
teach.body: Tailoring adapts PRINCE2 to the project's environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and level of risk. It changes HOW the method is used: processes, practices, roles, management products and terms. It never removes a principle or breaks a role rule. In the exam, good tailoring makes controls proportionate; bad tailoring quietly drops something the method depends on.

head: Element
Tailoring that fits
Example
rows: Light directing on a small project
Add a coach for an agile supplier
Brief and business case in one

teach.body: Formally: PRINCE2 is tailored so that the method fits the project, for example aligning with the business processes that govern it, and so that controls fit the project's scale, complexity, importance, team capability and risk, such as the frequency and formality of reports and reviews. In plain English: as much control as this project needs, in the language and formats this organization uses, and no less.

teach.caption: Role rules still apply when tailoring: one executive, never combined with the project manager, and assurance independent of the project manager.

teach.note: Each influence explains a particular tailoring choice. Pick the influence that matches the action in the stem.

items: Fernhollow's directors know the factory but not projects, and the recipe work runs in two-week cycles with a design agency. Nadia Osei (PM) leads 'agree the tailoring requirements' in initiation.
She adds a coach to help chefs, agency and board combine two-week cycles with PRINCE2 stages: an added role, appropriate.
She proposes weekly highlight reports in the trials stage, where food safety risk peaks, and fortnightly ones elsewhere: proportionate controls, appropriate.
The managing director suggests acting as executive AND project manager to speed things up: a broken role rule, not tailoring. Every choice goes into the PID for the board to approve.

teach.text: Tailoring is not omission. Dropping a principle (for example, no stage-end check on whether the project is still worth doing) or breaking a role rule (executive combined with PM; project support or the PM doing assurance) is never 'appropriate tailoring', however the option dresses it up.

items: Tailor processes, practices, roles, management products and terms to the environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and risk.
Purposes: the method fits the project, and controls fit its scale, complexity, importance, team capability and risk.
Principles cannot be tailored away; role rules still apply.
The PM leads 'agree the tailoring requirements' in initiation; tailoring is documented, recorded in the PID and approved by the board.

summary: You can now judge whether a tailoring decision is appropriate by checking that it keeps every principle and role rule, fits the project's scale, team and risk, and is documented and agreed. You can also name the influence or purpose that explains a particular choice.

A.q: Carrowford City Council's events manager is the project manager for its first half marathon; she attended a PRINCE2 7 Foundation course this year and has run only small events before. In initiation she proposes, and the board agrees, weekly highlight reports during the build-up stage instead of the council's usual monthly ones, recorded in the PID. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because tailoring lets the project manager set reporting without involving the board
Yes, because controls should fit the project's scale, team capability and level of risk
No, because the frequency of highlight reports is fixed by the method for every project
No, because more frequent reporting adds to the burden that manage by exception reduces
A.why: One purpose of tailoring is that project controls fit the project's scale, complexity, importance, team capability and risk, including how often reports are made (2.7). An inexperienced team on a high-profile event justifies more frequent reports.

whyNot.0: Tailoring is documented and agreed, and the board approves it in the PID; here the board did agree, but that is not why it is appropriate.
whyNot.2: Report frequency is exactly the kind of control that tailoring adjusts.
whyNot.3: Manage by exception does save senior management time, but a short, high-risk build-up with a new PM needs closer control.

A.q: Tarnside College starts a separate small project to replace the signage in one teaching block, with a budget of £18,000 and a six-week timescale. The project manager produces one short document that combines the project brief and the business case, and the board accepts it. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because a small, low-value project may merge the brief and the business case
Yes, because a project this small has no need of a business justification
No, because the business case has to be a separate product from the brief
No, because merging management products breaks the focus on products principle
A.why: Management products can be merged, and small, low-value projects may combine the project brief and business case in one simple document (2.7, 5.4.5). The justification is still there.

whyNot.1: Every project needs business justification; the principle cannot be tailored away. Merging keeps the case, it does not remove it.
whyNot.2: Products can be merged, split or renamed as part of tailoring; separation is not required.
whyNot.3: Focus on products concerns the project's outputs and their quality; merging two management products does not breach it.

A.q: Calderbrook's online permit service is being built by a supplier that uses Scrum in two-week sprints, but the council's board members and staff have never worked this way. The project manager proposes adding a coach to help the council's people work with the supplier's sprints inside the PRINCE2 stages. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because the coach could also act as project assurance for the supplier
Yes, because roles can be added when a supplier uses its own agile method
No, because the PRINCE2 set of roles is fixed and cannot be extended
No, because the supplier's delivery manager already runs the Scrum team
A.why: Roles can be combined, split or added; adding a coach where a supplier uses its own agile framework is a standard example of tailoring (2.7).

whyNot.0: Assurance is the board's responsibility and is a separate decision; it does not explain why a coach is needed.
whyNot.2: Roles can be added as part of tailoring; the set is not fixed.
whyNot.3: The delivery manager leads the supplier's team, but the gap is the council's people working with that method.

B.q: At Fernhollow Foods the managing director issued the mandate and signs off all large investments. To speed up decisions on the launch, she proposes to act as both the executive and the project manager. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because roles can be combined to suit a small, family-owned organization
Yes, because the executive is the single point of accountability for the project
No, because the executive and project manager roles must not be combined
No, because a managing director is too senior to run a project day to day
B.why: Roles can be combined when tailoring, but the role rules still apply: the executive and project manager roles are never combined (2.7, 6.2.4).

whyNot.0: Many roles can be combined, but this particular combination is ruled out whatever the organization's size.
whyNot.1: The executive is the single point of accountability, which is a reason to keep that role separate from day-to-day management.
whyNot.3: Seniority is not the test; the method rule is that these two roles stay separate.

B.q: At Wenmoor Community Health the board wants to keep the team small. It proposes that the project officer who maintains the registers and arranges meetings, acting as project support, should also carry out user assurance for the senior user. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because roles can be combined when people and money are short
Yes, because the senior user stays accountable when assurance is delegated
No, because project support must be kept separate from project assurance
No, because user assurance must be carried out by someone from outside
B.why: Project assurance cannot be done by the project manager, team members or project support, and support must be kept separate from assurance (6.2.4). Tailoring does not change this rule.

whyNot.0: Combining roles is allowed within the rules, and this combination breaks one of them.
whyNot.1: The senior user does stay accountable, but that does not make project support an acceptable choice.
whyNot.3: Assurance can be done by board members, by people from the wider business or by external parties; it does not have to be external.

B.q: Brennan Mutual's change framework talks about 'gate reviews' and 'monthly change updates'. In initiation the project manager uses these names for the end stage report and the highlight report, and sets out the mapping to the PRINCE2 terms in the PID. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Tailor to suit the project, because controls should match team capability and risk
Learn from experience, because the society's framework reflects its earlier projects
Focus on products, because each report is a management product with a description
Tailor to suit the project, because the method can use the organization's own terms
B.why: Terminology is one of the things that can be tailored, so the method fits the organization's business processes and language (2.7).

whyNot.0: Fitting controls to capability and risk is a purpose of tailoring, but renaming reports does not change any control.
whyNot.1: The framework may reflect past learning, but the action is adopting its vocabulary.
whyNot.2: The reports are management products, but renaming them is tailoring, not product definition.

C.q: On Carrowford's half marathon the race date is fixed and the cabinet has committed to the event. The executive proposes that, to save time, the board will not consider at stage ends whether the event is still worth running, and the project manager records this as tailoring. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because a fixed date means a check on whether to continue adds no value
Yes, because tailoring can simplify processes such as directing a project
No, because the stage-end decision belongs to the business layer, not the board
No, because a principle cannot be tailored away, and justification is revalidated
C.why: Principles are not tailored: all seven must be applied. Ensure continued business justification requires the case to be revalidated through the project (2.1, 2.7).

whyNot.0: A fixed date limits the options, but costs, entries and risks still change, and the event could stop being worthwhile.
whyNot.1: Processes can be simplified, but removing the justification check drops a principle rather than simplifying a process.
whyNot.2: Authorizing the next stage is a project board decision in directing a project.

C.q: At Wenmoor Community Health the board members work across three localities and have clinic commitments. The project manager proposes that highlight reports are shared through an online dashboard and that stage-end reviews are held by video call, with each decision documented. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because the formality and format of reports and reviews can be fitted to the project
Yes, because a board using video calls does not need to make formal stage-end decisions
No, because the board should meet in person to authorize a stage or exception plan
No, because highlight reports should keep the document format set out in the manual
C.why: Tailoring lets controls fit the project, including the frequency and formality of reports and reviews, and management products can take different formats (2.7). The decisions are still made and recorded.

whyNot.1: The board still makes formal decisions; only the meeting format has changed.
whyNot.2: Nothing in the method requires a face-to-face meeting; what matters is that the decision is made and documented.
whyNot.3: Management products can be given different formats, such as a dashboard.

C.q: On Calderbrook's permit project, the project manager and the supplier's delivery manager agree in passing that the supplier's sprint review notes will replace checkpoint reports. Nothing is written into the PID or the work package description, and the board has not been told. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because sprint reviews give the PM the status that checkpoint reports provide
Yes, because team managers decide for themselves how they report to the PM
No, because tailoring decisions should be documented and agreed in the PID
No, because checkpoint reports cannot be swapped for any other format
C.why: Tailoring, including any deviation from the standard method, must be documented and agreed; it is recorded in the PID, which the board approves (2.7).

whyNot.0: The swap itself might be sensible, but an undocumented, unagreed change is not appropriate tailoring.
whyNot.1: Checkpoint arrangements are agreed between the PM and team manager in the work package description, within the controls in the PID; here nothing was written down at all.
whyNot.3: Products can take different formats when tailoring; the problem is that it was not documented or agreed.

reteach.title: Fit it, never strip it
reteach.question: Picture a tailor taking in a suit: the cut changes, but the jacket still has both sleeves. What may change in PRINCE2, and what must stay?

blocks.h: The cut changes, the garment stays
blocks.body: You may resize the controls (report frequency, formality, formats), rename things, merge or split products, simplify processes and add or combine roles. You may not remove a principle, combine the executive with the project manager, or let the project manager or project support carry out assurance. And every change is written down and agreed, not done quietly.

blocks.text: An option that says 'Yes, because roles can be combined' is a classic lure when the combination breaks a rule. Check the specific combination before accepting the general statement.

explain.body: Tailoring is triggered by influences: a commercial customer and supplier, a programme context, a supplier's own framework, the organization's standards. The best answer names the influence that matches the action.

head: Influence
Typical response
rows: Align with two or more quality systems

test.q: Tarnside College has a design-and-build contract with a contractor that runs its own certified quality system. In initiation the project manager aligns the project's quality checks and records with the contractor's system, so that both sides use the same inspection records. Which statement explains why this is an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle?
options: A commercial relationship can mean aligning with more than one quality system
Management products can be merged when a project is small and of low value
Roles can be added when a supplier works with its own agile framework
Controls should be more frequent where the project team is inexperienced
test.why: Where there is a commercial customer and supplier relationship, the project may need to align its processes, practices and documents with two or more quality systems (2.7).

whyNot.1: This is a large capital project, and nothing is being merged; the action aligns with the contractor's quality system.
whyNot.2: The contractor's system is a quality system, not an agile framework, and no role is being added.
whyNot.3: Report frequency is a different tailoring choice and does not explain aligning inspection records.

explain.body: The project manager may also be team manager and project support. What the PM can never take on is the executive role or project assurance. Project support also cannot do assurance.

test.q: Calderbrook's project management office has two people. On the permit project, the project manager also leads the council's own small integration team as its team manager and keeps the registers herself. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because the project manager may also carry out project assurance on a small team
Yes, because the project manager may also hold the team manager and support roles
No, because the project manager role should not be combined with any other role
No, because the ICT infrastructure manager has to be the integration team manager
test.why: Roles can be combined within the rules: the project manager may also act as team manager and provide project support (2.7, 6.2.4).

whyNot.0: The project manager can never carry out project assurance; that is not what is happening here in any case.
whyNot.2: The PM role should not be SHARED between people, but it may be combined with team manager and support roles.
whyNot.3: Who leads a team is a choice, not a rule; the method does not require the ICT manager to be team manager.

explain.body: The project manager leads 'agree the tailoring requirements' in initiating a project. Tailoring, and any departure from the organization's standard method, is documented, recorded in the PID and approved by the board when it authorizes the project.

test.q: In initiation at Fernhollow Foods, the project manager writes the tailoring for the launch into the PID: an added coach role and the company's word 'phase' in place of 'stage'. The board approves it when it authorizes the project. Which statement explains why this is an appropriate action for the 'agree the tailoring requirements' activity?
options: Tailoring is decided by the business layer before the project starts up
Tailoring is set by the team managers who will use the management products
Tailoring is documented and agreed, and approved by the board with the PID
Tailoring is set by project assurance because it is independent of the PM
test.why: Tailoring decisions must be documented and agreed; they are recorded in the PID and approved by the project board when it authorizes the project (2.7, 15.4.1).

whyNot.0: The business layer may set standards, but the tailoring for this project is agreed in initiation, led by the PM.
whyNot.1: Team managers may be consulted, but they do not set the project's tailoring.
whyNot.3: Project assurance can advise, but it does not set the tailoring; the board approves it.

explain.body: Controls fit the risk and the team. A high-risk stage or a new team may need more frequent, more formal reporting; a low-risk stage run by an experienced manager may need less. Either way the board agrees it.

test.q: On Brennan Mutual's data centre exit, the project manager is an experienced PRINCE2 7 Practitioner. For the low-risk decommissioning stage she proposes monthly highlight reports in place of fortnightly ones, and the board agrees and records it. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM may change reporting frequency without the board's agreement
Yes, because the frequency of reports can be matched to the stage's risk and team
No, because highlight reports must stay at one frequency for the whole project
No, because the final stage of a project needs more reports than earlier stages
test.why: Controls should fit the project's scale, complexity, importance, team capability and risk, including how often reports are made (2.7). The change was agreed by the board.

whyNot.0: Tailoring is documented and agreed; the board did agree here, and its agreement is needed.
whyNot.2: Report frequency can vary to suit each stage's risk.
whyNot.3: There is no rule that the final stage needs more reports; it depends on the risk of the work.
